title: Regular Expressions
intro: A **regular expression** (regex) is a small pattern language for text. The `re` module searches with it: `re.search` finds the first match, `re.findall` finds them all, `re.fullmatch` checks a whole string and `re.sub` replaces matches. Write patterns as raw strings (`r"..."`) so backslashes reach `re` unchanged.

questions.prompt: `\d` is a digit, `\w` a letter, digit or underscore, `\s` a space. `+` means one or more, `*` zero or more, `?` optional, `{3}` exactly three. Brackets `( )` make a **group** you can pull out.
questions.exampleCode:
import re

text = "Room 12B opens at 09:30, room 7 at 10:15."
print(re.findall(r"\d\d:\d\d", text))     # ['09:30', '10:15']

m = re.search(r"Room (\d+)(\w?)", text)
print(m.group(0), m.group(1), m.group(2))  # Room 12B 12 B
questions.explanation: `group(0)` is the whole match; `group(1)` onwards are the brackets, left to right.

questions.code:
import re

print(re.findall(r"\d+", "Order 66 shipped 3 boxes on day 12"))
questions.explanation: `findall` returns every match as a string, in order.

questions.prompt: Write `find_emails(text)` that returns a list of the email addresses in `text`, in order. An address has a name, `@`, and a domain with at least one dot.

tests.name: found
tests.code: assert find_emails('Write to ana@example.com or ben.lee@mail.example.org.') == ['ana@example.com', 'ben.lee@mail.example.org'], 'Find both addresses, without the full stop at the end.'

tests.name: not addresses
tests.code: assert find_emails('No address: @nope, x@y, plain text') == [], 'Text without a real address gives [].'

questions.hint: Name: `[\w.+-]+`. Then `@`. Then a word, followed by one or more `.word` parts: `(?:\.[\w-]+)+`.
questions.explanation: `(?: )` groups without capturing, so `findall` still returns whole addresses. Real email rules are looser — this is a practical pattern, not a perfect one.

questions.prompt: Write `parse_iso(text)` that turns `"2025-10-29"` into the tuple `(2025, 10, 29)` of ints. Return `None` if the **whole** text isn't in that `YYYY-MM-DD` form.

tests.name: valid
tests.code: assert parse_iso('2025-10-29') == (2025, 10, 29), 'Return a tuple of three ints.'

tests.name: invalid
tests.code: assert parse_iso('29/10/2025') is None and parse_iso('2025-10-29!') is None and parse_iso('x2025-10-29') is None, 'Anything not exactly YYYY-MM-DD returns None.'

questions.hint: `re.fullmatch` with three groups; `m.groups()` gives them as a tuple of strings.
questions.explanation: `fullmatch` must cover the whole text, so extra characters at either end fail.

questions.prompt: Why write regex patterns as raw strings, like `r"\d+"`?

options.text: Python leaves the backslashes alone, so `re` sees them
They ignore upper and lower case

questions.hint: Think about what a plain string does with `\`.
questions.explanation: In a normal string, `\b` would become a backspace character before `re` ever sees it. Raw strings keep every backslash.

questions.prompt: `first_tag` should be `<b>`, but it grabs the whole string. Fix the pattern.
questions.starterCode: import re html = "bold and italic" first_tag = re.search(r"<.*>", html).group()
questions.solution: import re html = "bold and italic" first_tag = re.search(r"<.*?>", html).group()
questions.hint: `.*` is **greedy**: it takes as much as it can.
questions.explanation: Adding `?` (`.*?`) makes it lazy: it stops at the first `>`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the group name so `user` is the part before the `@`.
questions.template:
import re

m = re.search(r"(?P<___>[\w.]+)@", "ana@example.com")
user = m.group("user")
questions.hint: The name in `(?P<name>...)` must match the one in `group(...)`.
questions.explanation: Named groups make patterns easier to read than counting brackets.

questions.prompt: Write `mask_phones(text)` that hides phone numbers like `912 345 678`, keeping only the last three digits: `*** *** 678`.

tests.name: one
tests.code: assert mask_phones('Call 912 345 678 today') == 'Call *** *** 678 today', 'Mask the first six digits.'

tests.name: other numbers
tests.code: assert mask_phones('Order 1234 for 3 people') == 'Order 1234 for 3 people', 'Leave other numbers alone.'

questions.hint: Capture the last three digits with a group and put them back with `\1` in the replacement.
questions.explanation: `re.sub` can reuse groups in the replacement: `\1` is the first group.

questions.prompt: `re.split` splits on a pattern. What does this print?
questions.hint: Split at a comma or semicolon, plus any spaces after it.
questions.explanation: One pattern copes with mixed separators that `str.split` can't.

questions.prompt: Log lines look like `2025-10-29 14:03:11 ERROR Disk full`. Write `parse_log(line)` returning a dict with keys `date`, `time`, `level` and `message` (all strings), or `None` if the line doesn't fit.
questions.solution:
import re

LOG = re.compile(r"(?P<date>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}) (?P<time>\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) (?P<level>[A-Z]+) (?P<message>.+)")

def parse_log(line):
    m = LOG.fullmatch(line.strip())
    return m.groupdict() if m else None

tests.name: valid
tests.code: assert parse_log('2025-10-29 14:03:11 ERROR Disk full') == {'date': '2025-10-29', 'time': '14:03:11', 'level': 'ERROR', 'message': 'Disk full'}, 'Split the line into date, time, level and message.'

tests.name: invalid
tests.code: assert parse_log('Disk full') is None and parse_log('') is None, 'Lines that do not fit return None.'

questions.hint: Named groups plus `m.groupdict()` give you the dictionary directly.
questions.explanation: `re.compile` once, use many times — tidy when the same pattern runs over thousands of lines.
